title: The enemy of my enemy
hook: The enemy of my enemy is my friend. What does that force on a whole group?

knows: the saying "the enemy of my enemy is my friend"
doesNotKnow: that if every group of three is balanced, the whole group must split into at most two camps

misconception: A friend-and-enemy network can settle into several mutually hostile camps (three or more), or the saying alone does not say how many camps there can be.
objective: The learner can explain that when every trio of a fully connected friend/enemy group is balanced, the group is one camp or two (friends inside, enemies across), because three camps always contain a trio of three enemies: on five people, 3 camps leave at least 3 unbalanced trios.

claims.text: A trio is balanced if it has three friend (+) pairs, or one friend pair and two enemy (−) pairs; equivalently, its three signs multiply to +.
claims.source: Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 5 §5.1 (§ unconfirmed: from the table of contents, the book page returned a proxy 403 to the category manager). Code: unbalancedTrios() in src/demos/math/enemy-of-my-enemy/Demo.tsx (product of the three signs < 0). Address: predict question, stage rule line.

claims.text: Among the 1,024 friend/enemy settings of five people (10 pairs), 16 have every trio balanced: 1 is one camp (all friends) and 15 are two camps; every one of the 16 is a clean camp split (friends inside, enemies across).
claims.source: Node enumeration of all 2^10 sign settings with the lesson's exact rule (builder script, session scratchpad eme-check.mjs; brief 2 check by cm-math-discrete gives the same 16 = 2^(5-1)). Output: balanced 16, one camp 1, two camps 15, balanced but not a camp split 0. Address: reveal paragraphs 2 and 3 ('all 16 balanced settings are camp splits', 'one camp or two') for five people; stage readout 'not camps' never co-occurs with 0 unbalanced. | v4 (2026-10-14, demo-builder, W-574 learner r9): sentence cut from the reveal for the 90-word budget (111 -> 80); told context, learner r9 named it as a cut candidate. Not learner-visible. Withdrawn.

claims.text: In a camp split, the only unbalanced trios are those with one person from each of three different camps: such a trio has three enemy pairs. A trio inside one camp is + + +, and a trio with two in one camp is one + and two −, both balanced.
claims.source: Case analysis of the definition (c1); confirmed by node over all camp splits of 5 people. Address: reveal paragraph 1 ('Each takes one person from each camp, so all three pairs are −', after the learner's own unbalanced trios, e.g. ADE, BDE, CDE) and paragraph 2 ('a trio with one person from each is an unbalanced trio of three enemies'). Reworded 2026-10-14 by demo-builder for the told-vs-shown ruling; meaning unchanged, needs fact-checker re-read. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-5): re-read after the told-vs-shown rewording; VERIFIED stands. Each has one person from each camp: three − pairs.' (was 'Each takes one person from each camp, so all three pairs are −')), followed by 'So three camps never balance, and balanced means one camp or two.' Three camps of 5 leave 3 (3|1|1) or 4 (2|2|1) such trios, so the reveal always lists them (<= 4). Each has one person from each camp: three − pairs. 'So three camps never balance' follows.

claims.text: With five people in three non-empty camps, at least 3 trios are unbalanced: a 3-1-1 split leaves 3 and a 2-2-1 split leaves 4. Four camps leave 7, and all enemies (five camps) leaves all 10.
claims.source: Node enumeration over all 3^5 camp labellings with three non-empty camps (3-1-1: 3; 2-2-1: 4) and over all camp splits of the 1,024 settings (unbalanced by number of camps: 1 → 0, 2 → 0, 3 → 3 or 4, 4 → 7, 5 → 10). Address: reveal paragraph 2 ('at least 3', 'all 10'); stage readout 'Unbalanced'. | v4 (2026-10-14, demo-builder, W-574 learner r9): sentence cut from the reveal for the 90-word budget (111 -> 80); told context, learner r9 named it as a cut candidate. Not learner-visible. Withdrawn.

claims.text: On the stage, the '3 camps' preset is ABC | D | E with 3 of 10 trios unbalanced, and flipping D–E to friends makes ABC | DE with 0; starting from all enemies (10 unbalanced), making A–B, B–C, A–C friends gives ABC | D | E (3), and then D–E gives ABC | DE (0).
claims.source: Node replay of the QA path with the lesson's rules (scratchpad eme-check.mjs): start 10; AB 7 (AB|C|D|E); BC 6 (mixed); AC 3 (ABC|D|E); DE 0 (ABC|DE); AD 3; AE 4; BD 5; BE 4; CD 3 (all mixed); CE 0 (ABCDE); preset 3 camps 3 (ABC|D|E). Address: reveal paragraph 1 quotes the learner's own reached states.

claims.text: Balance theorem: if every trio of a complete friend/enemy network is balanced, then either everyone is friends or the people split into two groups, friends inside and enemies across; it holds for any number of people (reveal: 'This is the balance theorem, and it holds for any number of people.').
claims.source: Proof sketch: pick any person P; put P's friends with P and P's enemies in the other group. Balanced trios force friends inside each group and enemies across, for any n. n = 5 checked by enumeration (c2; fact-checker pass 38: 1,024 sign settings, 16 balanced, all one or two camps). | Before the 2026-10-15 rewording: Easley & Kleinberg (2010) ch. 5 §5.2 (§ unconfirmed), which attributes the result to Harary and to Cartwright and Harary (1956): D. Cartwright and F. Harary, 'Structural balance: a generalization of Heider's theory', Psychological Review 63(5), 277-293 (1956). Attribution and year unverified by the builder (could not open the source); the fact-checker confirms. Not empirical; the n = 5 case is checked by enumeration (c2). Address: reveal paragraph 3. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): The theorem statement is right (n = 5 re-enumerated: 16 balanced settings, all one or two camps) and the citation details are right: Cartwright D, Harary F (1956), "Structural balance: a generalization of Heider's theory", Psychological Review 63(5): 277-293, doi 10.1037/h0046049 (confirmed by search; full text not reachable through the proxy). But "is due to Cartwright and Harary (1956)" is a priority claim, and the two-group structure theorem for balanced signed graphs was first proved by Harary alone: F. Harary, "On the notion of balance of a signed graph", Michigan Mathematical Journal 2(2): 143-146 (1953); Cartwright and Harary (1956) carried it into social psychology. This lesson's own source line says E&K credits Harary as well as Cartwright and Harary. FIX (builder; this claim text and Demo.tsx reveal paragraph 3): claim "... it holds for any number of people; Harary proved it (1953), and Cartwright and Harary (1956) applied it to groups of people." Reveal: "This is the balance theorem (Harary, 1953; Cartwright and Harary, 1956), and it holds for any number of people." Then re-submit c6. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. Harary, 'On the notion of balance of a signed graph', Michigan Math. J. 2(2): 143-146 (1953) confirmed by search (one secondary source labels it 1954; journal details give 1953). Cartwright and Harary 1956 confirmed in NCM-1 (Psychol. Rev. 63(5): 277-293). The NCM-1 fix is applied in the claim and in reveal paragraph 3 ('Harary, 1953; Cartwright and Harary, 1956'). Theorem statement re-checked for n = 5 (16 balanced settings, all one or two camps). Primary papers not opened. | v4 (2026-10-14, demo-builder, W-574 learner r9 fit): reveal sentence now 'This is the balance theorem (Harary, 1953), and it holds for any number of people.' (the Cartwright and Harary 1956 citation cut for the stage-top crop). Claim text trimmed to what the learner reads. Needs re-check. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD. The theorem statement is right: own enumeration of all 1,024 sign settings of 5 people gives 16 balanced, all one or two camps, and the general proof (split by friends and enemies of any one person) holds for any n. The attribution 'Harary, 1953' is learner-visible. Earlier passes confirmed it by search snippet only; No source that supports it could be opened from this host: the cited hosts return proxy 403 or fail DNS, and only GitHub raw, PyPI and npm are reachable. I did not verify it from memory or from search snippets.

The learner-visible attribution 'Harary, 1953' needs Harary (1953), Michigan Math J 2(2): 143-146 (Project Euclid, not allow-listed) or Easley and Kleinberg ch. 5 (cs.cornell.edu, not allow-listed). recall.question: Six countries; every pair is allied or hostile, and every trio is balanced. Can they form three blocs, allied inside and hostile to every other bloc?
options: Yes, if the blocs are equal in size
Yes, any number of blocs works
recall.why: Take one country from each of three blocs: all three pairs are hostile, and a trio of three enemies is unbalanced. So balance allows one bloc or two, never three.
